narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 50.9% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped just above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your performance in the later years of college had the strongest influence. Even though your third-year decile of 5.0 sits close to the average of accepted students (5.79), the model interpreted it as a modest push toward a higher risk of failure. Your LSAT score of 30.5, noticeably below the 37.18 average of accepted applicants, was the second most important factor and pulled the prediction further toward failure. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.0, also below the accepted average of 3.23, added a third, smaller push in the same direction.

Interestingly, your first-year decile, family income in the upper-middle bracket, and plan to attend full-time had little impact on the outcome.

Taken together, these academic signals led the model to conclude your risk of not passing the bar on the first try was just high enough to deny admission. To improve your chances next time, focus on raising your LSAT score and strengthening your later-year grades, as these are the factors the model weighs most heavily. Consider retaking the LSAT and, if possible, additional coursework that can demonstrably lift your academic trajectory before reapplying.
